claim: Because independent 2026 creator-economy market estimates span $205B to $323B purely on definitional scope, any source quoting a single precise market-size figure is reporting a methodology choice rather than a measurement.
stance_target: Every precise creator-economy market-size figure quoted without its definitional scope
scope_conditions: Compiled July 2026; the spread arises from whether an estimate counts platform payouts and brand deals only, or adds creator-run commerce and tooling
quoted_support: The spread itself is the finding: any page quoting one precise figure is reporting a methodology choice, not a measurement.

claim: The ubiquitous '$480 billion by 2027' creator-economy figure is a Goldman Sachs projection dated 5 April 2023, built on a ~$250B base and ~50 million creators, and is routinely republished undated as if it were current measurement.
stance_target: Contemporary citations of the $480B creator-economy figure
scope_conditions: Goldman Sachs Insights 'Creator Economy Primer', 5 April 2023; a forecast built on a 10-20% CAGR assumption, not an observation
quoted_support: The number you have seen everywhere — 'the creator economy will approach $480 billion by 2027' — comes from a Goldman Sachs white paper dated April 5, 2023. At our publish date it is a three-year-old projection, yet nearly every 2026 statistics roundup still repeats it without the date.

claim: Goldman Sachs itself re-baselined the global creator population from ~50 million (April 2023) to ~67 million in 2025 heading to ~107 million by 2030, meaning the 50M figure still in wide circulation was superseded by its own originator.
stance_target: The '50 million creators globally' population estimate
scope_conditions: Goldman Sachs Global Investment Research note, 26 March 2025, reported via Net Influencer; ~10% CAGR assumption
quoted_support: Superseded by Goldman's own March 26, 2025 note, which puts the 2025 creator count at roughly 67 million, heading to a projected ~107 million by 2030. We flag the old number rather than silently swapping it.

claim: Creator payment concentration measurably widened between 2023 and 2025: the top 1% of creators captured 21% of all creator ad-payment volume in 2025, up from 15%, and the top 10% captured 62%, up from 53%.
stance_target: The claim that creator-economy growth concentrates rather than distributes income
scope_conditions: CreatorIQ State of Creator Compensation, published 21 January 2026, built on payment volume tracked through CreatorIQ's Creator Graph — i.e. payments routed through CreatorIQ-managed campaigns, not the whole market; sample size not stated; campaigns skew to brand-managed relationships and therefore likely exclude the lowest-earning creators entirely
quoted_support: The top 1% of creators captured 21% of all creator ad-payment volume in 2025, up from 15% in 2023; the top 10% captured 62%, up from 53%.

claim: Mean and median creator campaign earnings moved in opposite directions in 2025 — the average rose to $11.4K while the median fell to $3,000 from $3,500 — so the average runs roughly 3.8x the median and growth in the aggregate did not reach the typical creator.
stance_target: The objection that mean creator earnings figures conceal a falling median
scope_conditions: CreatorIQ campaign-payment distribution, 2025 data published 21 January 2026; per-campaign not annual; corroborated by TheWrap 14 January 2026; sample size not disclosed
quoted_support: The average earnings per brand campaign were $11.4K — but the median creator earned just $3,000 per campaign, down from a $3,500 median the prior year even as the average rose.

claim: Brand and agency investment in creator campaigns grew 171% year over year in 2025 while payments actually reaching creators grew 59%, implying the majority of new spend was captured upstream by platforms, agencies and top-tier talent.
stance_target: The objection that creator-economy growth figures do not describe creator income growth
scope_conditions: CreatorIQ, 21 January 2026; the upstream-capture interpretation is Digital Applied's inference from the two growth rates, not a CreatorIQ finding
quoted_support: It happened while brand and agency investment in creator campaigns rose 171% year over year — nearly three times the 59% growth in payments actually reaching creators.

claim: US creator annual earnings are distributed with 48.7% earning under $10,000, 45.6% earning $10,000-$100,000, and 5.7% earning $100,000 or more — roughly one in eighteen US creators reaching six figures.
stance_target: The share of creators earning a living wage
scope_conditions: The Influencer Marketing Factory 2026 Creator Economy Report, published February 2026; n=1,000 US creators surveyed plus analysis of 5M+ creator accounts; a self-selected vendor survey, and recruited from currently-active creators, so subject to survivorship bias; US only, does not generalise to Southeast Asia
quoted_support: 48.7% of US creators earn under $10,000 a year, 45.6% earn between $10,000 and $100,000, and 5.7% earn $100,000 or more.

claim: Two vendor surveys published within a month of each other report incompatible six-figure creator shares — 5.7% (Influencer Marketing Factory) and 11% (CreatorIQ) — and the source reproduces both without reconciling them.
stance_target: The reliability of any single vendor-survey figure for the share of creators reaching six-figure income
scope_conditions: Influencer Marketing Factory February 2026 (n=1,000 US creators) vs CreatorIQ January 2026 (survey pool size undisclosed, average annual income $44,293); differing populations and recruitment likely explain the gap, but neither source states its recruitment method
quoted_support: Average annual creator income in the CreatorIQ survey pool was $44,293 — yet only 11% of surveyed creators reported six-figure annual income.

claim: Roughly 3% of YouTubers capture 90% of net creator earnings on the platform, and the professional share is projected to fall from 3.0% in 2025 to 2.5% by 2030 because amateur entry outpaces professionalisation.
stance_target: The claim that platform earnings follow a power law that is worsening with entry
scope_conditions: Goldman Sachs research note, 26 March 2025, as summarised by Net Influencer — a second-hand summary, not the note itself; methodology described only as 'payout-share analysis of the YouTube ecosystem'; no sample size or data source disclosed
quoted_support: Roughly 3% of YouTubers capture 90% of net creator earnings on the platform (March 2025 note, as summarized by Net Influencer).

claim: The commonly-cited 'Patreon has paid creators $10 billion' figure is not a Patreon disclosure but an estimate from Graphtreon, a third-party tracker that aggregates publicly-visible creator pages.
stance_target: Attribution of Patreon cumulative-payout figures to Patreon itself
scope_conditions: Graphtreon tracker, accessed July 2026; scrapes only public creator pages, so systematically misses private and low-visibility creators
quoted_support: The ~$10B cumulative figure comes from Graphtreon, a third-party tracker that aggregates public creator pages — not from Patreon itself.

claim: The widely-repeated claim that the YouTube Partner Program has 3 million enrolled channels, up from 2 million in 2022, has no locatable YouTube-primary source despite appearing across dozens of aggregator pages.
stance_target: The YouTube Partner Program enrolment figure used to estimate monetised creator populations
scope_conditions: Verification pass conducted July 2026; an audited absence — the figure circulates without a traceable origin
quoted_support: Widely repeated, but our research pass could not locate a clean YouTube-primary post stating it directly. We print it below only as a widely-reported figure, not as company-confirmed.

claim: The '$44 billion influencer marketing market in 2026' figure has no named methodology behind it and is contradicted by cross-checked 2025 estimates clustering at $32.6B-$33B.
stance_target: The $44 billion influencer marketing market-size claim
scope_conditions: Verification pass July 2026; cross-checks are CreatorIQ ($32.6B, January 2026) and Statista (~$33B, global influencer marketing 2025)
quoted_support: No named methodology behind the precise forward-dated figure. The best cross-checked 2025 estimates cluster at $32.6B (CreatorIQ) to ~$33B (Statista); we excluded the $44B claim entirely.

claim: 76% of TikTok creator posts receive fewer than 1,000 views, indicating that the monetised creator economy described by earnings surveys sits atop a far larger base of accounts that no earnings figure describes.
stance_target: The objection that creator income surveys have a denominator problem
scope_conditions: The Influencer Marketing Factory 2026 Creator Economy Report, February 2026, from its analysis of 5M+ creator accounts; TikTok specifically; region not disaggregated in the reporting
quoted_support: 76% of TikTok creator posts receive fewer than 1,000 views — a reminder that the visible, monetized creator economy sits atop a much larger base of accounts the headline numbers never describe.

claim: YouTube's own disclosure — more than $100 billion paid to creators, artists and media companies over four years, plus $55 billion contributed to US GDP and 490,000+ FTE jobs supported in 2024 — is a company-verified aggregate that says nothing about how the pool is split.
stance_target: The evidentiary value of platform payout disclosures for questions about creator income distribution
scope_conditions: YouTube CEO Neal Mohan's annual priorities letter, 21 January 2026, first disclosed September 2025; a cumulative four-year aggregate covering creators, artists AND media companies together, so not decomposable to individual creator earnings; GDP and jobs figures are US-only, 2024
quoted_support: The pool is enormous and company-verified; the split of that pool is a barbell.

claim: The same barbell distribution appears across all three monetisation models — ad revenue, brand deals and subscriptions — but the three measurements use incompatible methodologies and are not directly comparable to one another.
stance_target: Cross-platform generalisation of creator income concentration
scope_conditions: Compiled July 2026 from Goldman Sachs payout-share analysis, CreatorIQ payment-volume share, and Graphtreon tracker-aggregated subscription revenue; the source itself flags the incomparability
quoted_support: Each row uses a different methodology (payout-share analysis, payment-volume share, tracker-aggregated subscription revenue), so the numbers are not directly comparable.

claim: 51.5% of US creators saw year-over-year earnings growth in 2025, a middle-tier signal that concentration statistics alone would conceal.
stance_target: The claim that creator-economy concentration means the typical creator is losing ground
scope_conditions: The Influencer Marketing Factory 2026 Creator Economy Report, February 2026, n=1,000 US creators; self-reported growth from a self-selected sample of currently-active creators — creators who quit during 2025 cannot appear in it, so the figure is survivorship-biased upward by construction
quoted_support: 51.5% of US creators saw year-over-year earnings growth in 2025 — a genuine middle-class signal that the concentration data alone would hide.
